The word has two meanings — a literal, technical one and a figurative one. Both are used in everyday English, and you need to know both to fully understand this word.

A dynamo is a machine that generates electricity by converting mechanical energy — the energy of physical movement — into electrical energy.

Here's the core idea: inside a dynamo, a coil of wire rotates within a magnetic field (or magnets rotate around a coil). This spinning motion disturbs the magnetic field in a way that pushes electric charges through the wire. That flow of charges is electricity. The source of the spinning can be anything — a steam engine, flowing water, a hand crank, or a spinning wheel.

The electricity a dynamo produces is called direct current (DC) — meaning the electricity flows in one direction only, like a steady stream in one direction. Batteries also produce DC.

This is different from the electricity in your home's wall sockets, which is alternating current (AC) — it rapidly reverses direction many times per second. A machine that generates AC specifically is called an alternator, not a dynamo.

So technically: a dynamo is a generator that produces DC. "Generator" is the broader word; "dynamo" is one specific type. In casual, everyday speech, people often use the two words interchangeably — and that's fine in non-technical contexts. Nobody will misunderstand you.

A familiar real-world example: The bicycle dynamo — the small device clamped beside a bicycle wheel. When the wheel spins, it drives this tiny machine, which produces electricity to power the bike's lights. No battery needed. The energy comes entirely from the motion of the wheel.

Large dynamos were also the backbone of early electrical power stations in the late 1800s, supplying electricity to entire cities for the first time in history.

This is the more common use in modern conversation, and it's the meaning you'll encounter most.

When you call a person a dynamo, you mean they have extraordinary energy, drive, and productivity — someone who seems to never tire, who is always moving, always working, and somehow gets far more done than the average person. They are a source of energy for everything around them.

The connection to the machine is vivid and precise: just as a dynamo continuously generates power that other things run on, a "dynamo person" continuously generates effort, ideas, and results that fuel a team, a project, or a whole organisation.

This usage is always a compliment. You would never use it to describe someone negatively. It carries a tone of admiration, even awe.

One important nuance: A dynamo isn't merely someone who is busy or restless — it implies effectiveness. The image is of someone who channels that energy into real, visible results. A person who runs around frantically without accomplishing much would not typically be called a dynamo. The word implies that the energy is productive.

• "My grandmother is a complete dynamo — she volunteers every morning, tends her garden in the afternoon, and is learning Spanish at 75."
  • "The new manager is a dynamo; she's already transformed the team in just three months."
  • "Don't let his quiet demeanor fool you — he's a dynamo once he gets to work."
  • "The startup's CEO is the kind of dynamo investors love: relentless, focused, and always delivering."
  • "The bicycle dynamo on his old bike has been powering the lights for twenty years without a single battery."
The one mental image that ties it all together

Think of the machine first: a dynamo doesn't consume energy — it generates it for others to use. That is precisely the quality the word transfers to a person. A dynamo-person is not someone who drains the room of energy; they are someone who produces it, who powers the people and projects around them. Whether machine or person, the core idea is always the same: an engine of output, running seemingly without end.
The plural is dynamos. You'll rarely see it, since the figurative use almost always refers to a single person being described.
